entry.gloss: note that does not belong to the chord
entry.def: A note that is not part of the chord sounding with it, usually a dissonance that decorates a chord tone. Non-chord tones are named by how they are approached and left: by step or leap, up or down, on a strong or weak beat. Also called a nonharmonic tone or embellishing tone, and in British books a non-harmonic or unessential note.

entry.gloss: steps between two chord tones in one direction
entry.def: A non-chord tone that fills the gap between two chord tones a third apart, approached and left by step in the same direction. Usually unaccented; two passing tones in a row can fill a fourth. Called a passing note in British English.

entry.gloss: passing tone on a strong beat
entry.def: A passing tone that falls on a beat or strong part of the beat, often where the chord changes, so that it sounds as a dissonance against the new chord before moving on by step.

figure.caption: C passes from D to B on the third beat, against the dominant chord.

entry.gloss: steps away from a chord tone and back
entry.def: A non-chord tone a step above (upper neighbor) or below (lower neighbor) a chord tone, approached from it by step and returning to it. Called an auxiliary note, or neighbour note, in British English.

entry.gloss: neighbor tone with a leap on one side
entry.def: A non-chord tone a step from a chord tone that is reached or left by leap instead of by step on both sides. The appoggiatura (leap, then step) and the escape tone (step, then leap) are often treated as its two kinds.

entry.gloss: upper and lower neighbors in a row around one note
entry.def: Two non-chord tones in a row that surround a chord tone: from the chord tone a step up, a third down, and a step up back to it, or the mirror image. Also called a double neighbor or neighbor group. Some books call it a cambiata, a word species counterpoint uses for a different figure.

entry.gloss: accented dissonance reached by leap, left by step
entry.def: A non-chord tone, usually accented, that resolves by step; the name is Italian for leaning. Kostka and Payne define it as approached by leap and left by step, usually in the opposite direction; others, following eighteenth-century usage, use the name for any accented dissonance that is not prepared and resolves by step, however it is approached. In Baroque and Classical scores it is often written as a small note.

figure.caption: The A is reached by a leap and falls by step to G, a chord tone.

entry.gloss: unaccented step away, then leap back the other way
entry.def: An unaccented non-chord tone approached by step and left by leap in the opposite direction, often decorating a falling step in the melody. Also known by its French name, échappée.

entry.gloss: note of the next chord sounding early
entry.def: A non-chord tone that sounds a note of the next chord just before that chord arrives, usually approached by step and on a weak part of the beat. The anticipated note is then repeated or held when the chord changes. Common in the soprano at cadences.

entry.gloss: held-over note that resolves down by step
entry.def: A note held over from one chord into the next, where it becomes a dissonance on the strong beat and then resolves down by step. Its three stages are the preparation, the suspension itself and the resolution. Suspensions are named by the intervals above the bass at the dissonance and the resolution, as in 4–3, 7–6 and 9–8; with the dissonance in the bass, 2–3.

figure.caption: C is prepared in the IV chord, held against the dominant, and resolves to B.

entry.gloss: the consonant note before a suspension
entry.def: The first stage of a suspension: the same note sounded as a consonance in the chord before, so that the dissonance arrives without a new attack. More generally, any dissonance that is preceded by the same note as a consonance is said to be prepared.

entry.gloss: suspended fourth resolving down to the third
entry.def: A suspension in which an upper voice forms a fourth above the bass and resolves down to the third, often over V at a cadence. The third of the chord should not sound in another voice at the same time.

entry.gloss: suspended seventh resolving down to the sixth
entry.def: A suspension in which an upper voice forms a seventh above the bass and resolves down to a sixth, so that the chord of resolution is in first inversion. Chains of 7–6 suspensions over a falling bass are common in Baroque music.

entry.gloss: suspended ninth resolving down to the octave
entry.def: A suspension in which an upper voice forms a ninth above the bass and resolves down to the octave, doubling the bass. Unlike other suspensions it keeps the compound number, so that it is not confused with the 2–3 suspension.

entry.gloss: suspension in the bass: second resolving to a third
entry.def: A suspension in the bass: the bass is held while an upper voice moves to form a second (or ninth) above it, and the bass then resolves down by step to make a third (or tenth). Also called a bass suspension.

entry.gloss: suspension that resolves up by step
entry.def: A suspension that resolves up instead of down, most often a leading tone held into the tonic chord and rising to the tonic, a 7–8 retardation.

A note held or repeated, usually in the bass, while the harmonies above it change, some of them clashing with it. Most pedal points are on the tonic or the dominant. A pedal point in an upper voice is called an inverted pedal. Often shortened to pedal.

figure.caption: A tonic pedal under I, IV, V and I in C major.
